title: Chapter 139 – The Second Side
html:
[The Lin Orchard – Lin Jian]

The tape runs for forty minutes, and none of them move.

It is the strangest sound Jian has ever heard in a cave. A man's voice, small and tinny and dry, filling a hall as wide as a barn with the ordinary noises of a human being thinking: a cough, a creak, the clink of a cup, the rustle of paper turned over. Sometimes there is a long pause, and he hears the hiss of the tape and the slow settle of a chair. Sometimes the voice laughs, helplessly, at its own phrasing. It does not sound like a god. It sounds like a tired man in a kitchen at three in the morning, trying to explain himself to his wife.

"I'll tell you what I can," says Ethan Cole. "Which isn't much. Let me start with the Order, since you've met them."

Jian sits on the dais step with his hands between his knees. Wenyuan has lowered himself onto a stone bench between two green pillars, with his staff across his lap. Yue stands very straight a pace behind, holding Pebble against her chest. The pale light of the hall falls on all of them evenly, like a lamp in an empty room.

"They aren't a conspiracy," says the voice. "I want that clear. I know what they've done. I know about the burned names, the Numbers, the Chain, the ones who sleep. I know it's monstrous. But they don't think they're monsters, and that matters, because the thing that makes monsters out of decent people is the belief that they're doing it for someone else."

A pause.

"When I built the loop, I left a set of instructions. Four lines, in a book, in a language I invented. I gave it to the first man I trusted. It said: Wait for the Operator. Keep him safe. When he is ready, bring him home. That's all. Four lines. I thought it was clear." A dry cough. "It was six hundred years ago. They've had a very long time to interpret it."

Wenyuan makes a small sound. Yue's hand moves on Pebble's fur.

"They interpreted safe as alive. They interpreted ready as willing. And they interpreted home as the Gate. I didn't mean that. I meant—" The voice stops. When it resumes it is lower. "I'm not going to tell you what I meant. Not here. But I'll tell you this. They have never once done anything I didn't, in some way, ask them to. I'm the one who built the thing that eats names. I'm the one who wrote the book. If you want to be angry at somebody, be angry at the man in this box."

* * *

"Here's the part you need," says the voice.

It has changed. The humor is gone. The words come slowly, one at a time, like stones set down in a stream.

"The Gate has a switch. I built it in the first year. It's a consent switch. The Operator walks through, and the restore happens. If the Operator doesn't walk, it doesn't. That was the point. That was the whole point. I didn't want anybody dragged." A breath. "I thought I was being careful.

"I wasn't. I missed something. I missed it for ninety years, and when I found it, it was too late to fix." The tape hisses. "The switch trips on death. If the Operator dies, near the Gate, within reach of the Dock, the restore happens anyway. No consent. No choice. The working copy stops, and the Gate does the next thing. It was a fail-safe. I put it in so that if something went wrong, the stored copy wouldn't be lost. I never thought it would become the rule."

Jian closes his eyes.

They carry the dying. He remembers Lan Ji's low voice in the Quiet School. Two men with plum-colored seals. They sat with him until dawn.

"So," says Ethan Cole, "this is the rule, kid. Don't die near the Gate. Not on the stair, not in the Dock, not in the hall. Stay a hundred li from any Dock if you can, and if you can't, don't die in it. The Order will take you if you do. They'll be gentle about it. They'll think they're giving you a gift." The voice cracks, very slightly. "I'm sorry. I'd give a great deal to have thought of it sooner."

Nobody speaks. In the stillness, Wenyuan lifts his head. A drip of water falls somewhere in the dark, loud as a bell. Pebble's tail flicks once against Yue's arm.

It is Jian who breaks the silence, in the end, with a sentence he did not know he was going to say. "I have been to three Docks," he says, to the empty hall, "and I have always been afraid of what the men in them would want from me. I never once thought to be afraid for them."

"You should not be," says Yue, very gently. "They were all you."

"That is exactly what frightens me."

Nobody answers. Then Wenyuan lifts his head.

"Is he saying," he says carefully, in a small steady voice, "that my son will be taken if he dies near that wall?"

"He is saying more than that, Father," says Jian.

"I know." The old man's eyes are very bright. "I am only asking him to say it plainly."

The box clicks and hisses. The tape rolls on, deaf to the question, and Ethan Cole says from six hundred years away:

"There'll be witnesses. There always are. Somebody who loves you, probably, standing behind you with their hand on your shoulder. I want you to hear this too. Whoever you are."

* * *

"I know what you think I did," says the voice.

It is very quiet now. The hiss of the tape is almost louder than the words.

"You think I made a copy of myself, and put it in a child, and let it grow up believing it was a person. You think I treated a boy like a cloak I could put on and take off. And you're right. That's exactly what I did. I'm not going to tell you it was a kindness. I'm not going to tell you it was necessary, though it was. I'm going to tell you that I know the child is a person. I've known it since the second loop. I've known it every time I've been restored and woken in a white room with a tag on my wrist and a nurse saying welcome back, Mr. Cole, and felt, underneath the relief, the particular silence where someone used to be."

Wenyuan's lips are moving. Jian cannot tell whether he is praying or counting.

"Here is the thing I can't undo," says Ethan. "The child exists. He exists because of the loop. He has a mother and a father, and he's loved, and he's been loved well, by people I'll never meet. And when I'm restored, he stops. Not dies. Stops. The way a song stops. And there is nobody in the first world who can remember him, because he was never in the first world to begin with." A long silence. "I think about that every day. I think about it in the shower. I think about it when I try to sleep.

"So here's what I've done. It's the only thing I could think of. I've built a way to let the child choose."

Jian's eyes open.

"The third stone," says the voice. "You've been told what it does. It completes the Gate. It lets the Gate go both ways. Everybody thinks that means restore. It does. But it also means send. For one use, and only one, with the door open, you can send a single message from the ancient side to the first. To the stored copy. To me." The voice gathers itself. "You can say anything. Anything at all. I don't know what you'll say. That's the point. I can't tell you; I'm not the one standing there. The child is. The child is the only one who knows."

Wenyuan has risen from the bench. He is standing quite straight, gripping the staff, and his face is gray.

"So that is what this is," he says. "A door that lets a boy speak to the man who made him."

"A door that lets me listen," says the voice, from the box, as though in answer. "I've been talking for six hundred years. I'd like, just once, to be told off."

* * *

When the tape ends there is a long soft click, and the hall is silent.

Jian does not move. He sits on the dais step with the dust of the hall on his cloak and the weight of his own breathing in his chest, and he feels nothing at all, and that frightens him more than grief would.

It is Wenyuan who speaks first.

"Jian."

"Yes, Father."

"Stand up."

He stands. The old man comes forward, slowly, across the polished floor, with his staff tapping, and stops in front of him. He is smaller than Jian remembers. His shoulders are bent. He has to tilt his head back to look up. His eyes in the green light are wet, but they are perfectly steady.

"You will listen to me now," says Wenyuan. "I am eighty-six. I have outlived my parents and three of my children's teachers. I do not understand what that box said about copies. I do not need to. I understand one thing." He lifts his cold gloved hand and lays it, flat, against Jian's chest, over the heart. "A boy was born in the winter after the Orchard fell. He weighed like a stone. He did not cry. His mother did not sleep for three days for fear he was ill. He learned to walk on a floor I laid with my own hands. I have called him by a name every night of his life that he does not now remember. That is the boy I am talking about."

"Father—"

"He is my son."

It is said very quietly. It is said without any heat. It is said in the voice of a man reading a ledger entry, a fact among other facts, plain and enormous and not to be argued.

"Whoever the man in the box may be, he is not my business. He built a room. He did not put the child in my arms. I did that. Qinghe did. We did it with our hands, over a great many nights, in a house with a leaking roof." His hand presses harder. "And if that man comes to me tomorrow, or in a thousand years, and says that my son is a thing that can be put down, I will tell him what I am telling you now."

"What?"

"That he is mistaken." The old man's mouth trembles, and then, astonishingly, firms into a smile. "I am a very stubborn farmer. It is the only thing I am any good at."

Jian cannot speak. He bows his head. After a moment he feels his father's other hand, cold in its glove, come up and cup the back of his skull as it did when he was a child, and he leans into it, and stays there for as long as anyone lets him.

* * *

When Wenyuan has sat down again, Jian climbs the dais and stands in front of the box.

It looks smaller than it did. Its dull casing is nicked and pitted. The scrap of paper taped to the front has curled at the corners. He has the odd sense that he is standing in front of a very old dog that has been waiting at a gate for sixty years. He puts his hand on the metal. It is faintly warm.

"Mr. Cole," he says.

His own voice sounds strange in the hall. He clears his throat and begins again.

"I am not going to say it to you. Not yet. I do not know what the message is." He swallows. "I only wish to say that I heard you. All of it. I want you to know that someone did."

The box ticks. A pale light blinks once on its grill, orange, and goes out.

"I am not angry," he says. "I thought I would be. I have been angry for a long time, at a great many things. At the Registry. At the Order. At the Door that takes my memories one at a time and gives nothing back. I thought that when I found you, I would have a great deal to say." He laughs, shakily. "I find I have only one thing. I would like to ask you what it was like."

Silence. The hall hums.

"Being me. Being the child. Did you ever dream of it? Did you wake in your white room and remember a lamp?" He closes his hand around the casing. "My father says that I looked at it for an hour and did not cry. I have always wondered what I was thinking. I think now it may have been you. I think it may have been you, saying oh no, and what have I done."

He stops. His throat has closed.

"It is all right," he says, very low. "I have had a good life."

He takes his hand away. The box ticks once more. Then the orange light blinks, steady, twice, three times, like a man tapping on a table, and goes dark. The hall is still. Behind him, on the bench, Wenyuan has bowed his head.

* * *

Behind them Yue has gone to the far end of the hall.

She stands between two pillars carved with plum, looking at the wall, and Pebble sits at her feet, and neither moves. After a while Jian goes to join them. His sister does not turn. Her eyes are wet and enormous. Her hands are folded very tightly in front of her.

"There is something in the wall," she says.

"A seam?"

"A shelf." She points. "Behind the third pillar. Pebble found it."

He looks. There is a hairline crack in the white stone, no wider than a thread, and when he lays his palm on it the Door answers, calm and cool, the thin bright wire of a seam opening in his mind. He steps. Four units. When he comes back he is carrying a jar.

It is the same as the others, squat and black and sealed with wax. But this one is smaller, no larger than a man's two fists, and the brass tag on its shoulder is stamped not with a number but with a symbol: a single small ear, cut deep into the metal. A slip of creased paper lies beneath.

For the one who hears.

Not now. Not for years. But she will know.

—E.C.

Yue stares at the jar. She makes no move to take it.

"It is mine," she says.

"I think so."

"Why mine? I am nobody. I have no root. I am forty years behind a ledger of doors." Her voice shakes. "I am not even Foundation."

"You are the head of the Seat. You are the one who hears. You were the first to hear him, the first time, before the tape, before the Dock." He puts the jar into her hands. "He said bring someone who hears seams. I brought you. He did not say why."

"Perhaps he did not know."

"Perhaps." He smiles, a little. "But I think he did."

She holds the jar against her chest the way she once held a goat kid, and looks at the box on its stool at the end of the hall, and says in a very low voice, to nobody, "I would like to tell him that he writes a terrible letter."

"He would probably agree."

"I would like to tell him that anyway."

* * *

The ramp that leads up to the Mother Tree is long and shallow, and they take it slowly, because of Wenyuan.

The old man leans on Yue's arm. He does not speak. His breath comes short and thin, and every few paces he stops with his hand pressed flat against the green wall and looks at nothing. Jian walks a step behind, with the box's last orange blink still printed on the back of his eyes. Pebble trots ahead, tail up, ears swiveling.

"Mother will want to know," says Yue, at the third landing.

"Yes."

"All of it?"

"She will ask." He shifts the jar in his arms. "She has never once failed to ask."

"She will take it hard."

"She will take it the way she takes everything. She will say that it is nonsense, and then she will make soup, and then she will sit by the stove with her hands in her lap for a day and a night." He smiles without humor. "It is how she grieves. I used to think she was angry."

Yue is quiet. Her eyes are on the old man's bowed head. "Jian," she says. "May I ask something?"

"Of course."

"When you said, at the Dock, that you had been Ethan Cole for thirty-eight years. And Lin Jian for thirty-eight." She chooses her words carefully. "Which of them is speaking, now?"

He climbs three more steps before he answers. In the stillness, he can hear the old man's breathing, and his own, and the faint distant hum of the Mother Tree overhead, like a bee in a flower.

"I do not know," he says. "I used to think it mattered."

"And now?"

"Now I think that is what the Door is for. To find out." He shifts the jar again. "He said it himself. The child is the only one who knows what to say. If that is true, then the child had better get used to being asked."

Pebble stops. She stands rigid on the ramp in front of them, one paw lifted, her ears flat against her skull.

"Something is wrong," she says.

"What?"

"The seams are very loud." Her voice is tight. "Above us. In the grass. They are all pointing the same way. Like a hundred people turning their heads." She looks back at them with huge dark eyes. "Jian. Somebody has come."

* * *

They climb out into a blue twilight, and the Unkept are on their knees.

It is not the kneeling of men at prayer. It is the kneeling of men who have been struck. They are scattered across the dead grass at the foot of the Mother Tree, nine gray figures in the blue dusk, on their knees and elbows, with their hands over their heads. Lan Wen is flat on his face with his white eye staring at nothing. A pale mist is rising from the grass, thin and chill, carrying the faint sweet smell of crushed plum.

Jian steps off the stone slab, and stops.

They are standing in a ring.

There are perhaps two hundred of them. They stand perfectly still, shoulder to shoulder, in the half-light, in plain gray tunics with plum-colored seals at the collar. They carry no weapons. They breathe together. The air in the valley has thickened until it is difficult to draw breath. At the head of the ring, ten paces from the roots of the tree, a tall figure waits in a veil.

The Warden of the Roll does not move. His hands are folded in front of him. His long narrow sword hangs at his hip.

"Keeper," he says.

"Warden."

"Forgive the manner of it." The voice is the same dry, level, courteous one. Jian thinks that there is something in it that was not there before, a kind of fracture, a faint dissonance, as of a violin string kept too long under tension. "It was necessary. You have been very difficult to find."

"I was in a cellar."

"So I perceive." The veil tilts, slowly, toward Wenyuan, who has come up the last of the steps leaning on Yue's arm. "And this is your father."

Wenyuan straightens. He is a very old man in a patched cloak, in the dusk, in the ruin of the place he was born, facing two hundred silent clerks and a Golden Core cultivator. His gloved hands rest on the head of his staff. He looks, Jian thinks, like a man waiting for a ferry.

"Good evening," he says.

"Elder Lin." The Warden inclines his head. "I have a message for the Garden. I thought it best to deliver it here."

"Why here?"

"Because it is the place where it begins." The veiled figure raises one arm, slowly, and sweeps it across the dead valley, the meadow, the humps of the old foundations, the black tree. "This ground is the Second House's. It was always the House's. It was held for six hundred years by a family of farmers who did not know what they kept. They know it now." The arm falls. "The House has been generous. It has waited. It has held the Chain and fed the sleepers and kept the peace. It will do so no longer."

"What is it that you want?" Wenyuan asks.

"The Gate Stair. The Dock. The Roll. The Keeper." A pause. "And the dissolution of the Seat."

"The Seat."

"By midwinter. The Garden Hall will be given to the House's keeping. Your clan will be offered a place in the Second House's service, with a stipend and honors." The voice does not waver. "Those who refuse will be released with a month's grain."

"And if we refuse?"

"Then the House will take it," says the Warden. "And I will be the one to do it."

There is a silence. A thin wind moves the grass.

Wenyuan studies the veil for a long time. Then he turns his head and looks at Jian, quite calmly, and Jian sees that he is waiting. Not for permission. For the answer to a question he already knows.

Don't die near the Gate, thinks Jian. Don't let them carry you. Don't go home.

He steps forward.

He stands beside his father, in front of the Mother Tree, with his sister's hand on his sleeve and the Unkept rising one by one from the grass behind him, silent and gray, and he looks at the Warden's veil, and says, in the voice of a man who has made a decision a very long time ago and has only now found the courage to say it:

"No."

For a long moment nothing happens.

The Warden does not move. The two hundred clerks do not move. The wind drops, and in the sudden silence Jian hears the Mother Tree creak, once, deep in its black heart, like a ship at anchor. Then the veiled head tilts a fraction, with the exactness of a man marking a line in a ledger.

"I thought you might," says the Warden, softly.

"Then why ask?"

"Because it is the form." There is a faint, tired humor in the voice. "A Warden is obliged to ask. I have asked." He turns, slowly, with a rustle of gauze, and the ring of clerks opens before him like a door. "Midwinter, Keeper. The House will come for the stair at midwinter. It will come in good order, with all its clerks, and all its patience. You have two moons."

He walks away through the grass. At the edge of the ring he pauses, one hand on his sword hilt, and speaks without turning.

"I would give a great deal," he says, "to have you take the seat."

Then the mist swallows him, and the clerks follow in a silent gray file, and the valley is empty, and the Unkept are on their feet again, shaking, and Wenyuan is leaning on Yue with his staff trembling in his glove. A single apple falls from the Mother Tree with a soft thud and rolls to a stop at Jian's boot.

"Well," says the old man, breathless and cheerful. "Your mother will be furious we went without her."
